at.step: Bin packing: fit every item into as few fixed-size bins as possible. First-Fit Decreasing's rule is almost the simplest one imaginable — sort every item from largest to smallest, then drop each one into the first bin that still has room, opening a new bin only when nothing fits.

Dosa proved in 2007 exactly how far this simple rule can drift: the number of bins it uses is never more than eleven ninths of the true optimum, plus six ninths on top. Reproducing the standard tight construction directly — thirty items in four carefully chosen sizes — the rule uses eleven bins where the total volume alone already demands at least nine.

Here is a second, smaller instance, small enough to check every possible arrangement completely: eight items, capacity twelve, and First-Fit Decreasing reaches for four bins. Does checking every arrangement confirm that four bins is already the best anyone could do?
That volume floor isn't the same as a proved optimum, so here is the proof on this instance: eight items, and brute force proves three bins suffice, where the simple rule reaches for a fourth.

Longest-Processing-Time-first sorts the jobs from longest to shortest before assigning each one to whichever machine currently has the least work. Plain list scheduling does the identical assignment step, but skips the sorting — it takes the jobs in whatever order they already arrive in. Does that one difference, sorted or not, actually change the worst-case guarantee?

Graham's own tight family, reproduced and checked against a true, brute-force-proven optimum at every machine count from two through five: ratios of seven sixths, eleven ninths, five fourths and nineteen fifteenths — each one landing exactly on four thirds minus one over three times the machine count, to the decimal place.

Now the classic worst case for the unsorted version: enough unit-sized jobs to fill every machine evenly, submitted first, then one large job arriving last and landing on whichever machine happens to be least loaded — which, by then, is every machine equally. The result is a finishing time of nearly double the true optimum, brute-force-verified exactly. Sort those identical jobs first instead, and the same assignment rule lands precisely on the optimum.

at.step: Apache Spark's own file-splitting code names its algorithm directly in a comment: Next Fit Decreasing. Read closely, it only ever checks the single most recently opened partition for room — never any earlier one — closing it and starting fresh the moment the next file would overflow it. That is a cheaper relative of First-Fit-Decreasing, not the identical algorithm, and the eleven-ninths guarantee proved for First-Fit does not automatically carry over to it.

The 11/9·OPT + 6/9 bound is asymptotic, not absolute: at very small OPT (say OPT = 1 or 2) the additive +6/9 dominates and the ratio FFD/OPT can exceed 11/9 by a wide margin in relative terms, even though the bound itself always holds in absolute terms. This topic states the bound as written (an inequality on bin counts), not as a simplified ratio, to avoid implying a false absolute guarantee at small scales.

items.item: A lower bound computed purely from total volume (ceiling of total size over capacity) is itself a valid, cheap lower bound on OPT, but a strictly weaker one than OPT in general — this topic explicitly does not conflate 'volume bound equals 9' with 'OPT equals 9,' since a packing constraint (an item that is itself more than half the capacity, for instance) can force OPT above the volume bound even when the raw numbers would otherwise fit.

items.item: LPT's bound assumes identical (uniform-speed) machines; on unrelated or uniformly-related machines (different speeds per machine) neither LPT's rule nor its 4/3 bound directly applies, and a different algorithm family (not covered here) is needed — this topic's scope, per CHAPTER.md, is identical machines only, matching the syllabus line's own wording.

items.item: The list-scheduling worst-case instance (m(m-1) unit jobs then one job of size m) depends on the big job arriving dead last, after every machine is already tied at m-1 — a slightly different arrival order (the big job arriving first, say) would let list scheduling find the optimum trivially; the topic's claim is specifically about list scheduling's own worst case over all possible orders, not about every order being equally bad.

items.item: Spark's own 'Next Fit Decreasing' operates on a pre-sorted-by-descending-size file list upstream (in the real planner, not shown in FilePartition.scala itself) — this topic's examples.py reproduces only the partitioning step FilePartition.scala actually contains, and states plainly that the descending sort happens elsewhere in the real system, not inventing a sort step that isn't in the quoted source.

The 11/9 FFD guarantee and the 4/3 LPT guarantee are proved by entirely different techniques (a volume-and-counting argument for FFD; a direct case analysis on the largest job's position for LPT) despite both bounding against a computable lower bound on OPT — the topic's shared 'lower bound on OPT' framing is a unifying narrative device, not a claim that the two proofs share machinery.

First-Fit Decreasing's own name only promises the sorted variant; plain First-Fit (no sort) has a strictly weaker known bound (17/10, not 11/9), so the sorting step in FFD is doing real work for bin packing too, mirroring the LPT-vs-list-scheduling contrast this topic draws out for scheduling — this topic covers only the sorted (decreasing) variant for packing, matching the syllabus line's own wording.

items.item: Bin packing's decision version (does I fit in k bins?) is NP-complete, which is why no algorithm here is claimed to find the true optimum quickly; the brute-force check on the eight-item instance works only because that instance is small enough for exhaustive search to finish, not because brute force is itself a practical general algorithm.

items.item: Partitioning files for a distributed query engine and scheduling jobs onto executors are related but distinct problems from the chapter's own bin-packing and makespan-scheduling abstractions: a file split has a byte size (packing-like) while an executor task has a duration (scheduling-like), and Spark's own code quoted here is solving the packing-shaped problem, not the scheduling-shaped one, which this topic's syllabus clause keeps distinct rather than conflating.
